Gildas CLASS files

Pyspeckit is capable of reading files from some versions of CLASS. The
CLASS developers have stated that the GILDAS file format is private and
will remain so, and therefore there are no guarantees that the CLASS
reader will work for your file.

Nonetheless, if you want to develop in python instead of SIC, the
~pyspeckit.spectrum.readers.read_class module is probably the best way
to access CLASS data.

The CLASS file specification is incomplete, so much of the data reading
is hacked together. The code style is based off of Tom Robitaille's
idlsave package.

An example usage. Note that telescope and line are NOT optional keyword
arguments, they are just specified as such for clarity :

    n2hp = class_to_obsblocks(fn1, telescope=['SMT-F1M-HU','SMT-F1M-VU'],
        line=['N2HP(3-2)','N2H+(3-2)'])

This will generate a ~pyspeckit.spectrum.ObsBlock from all data tagged
with the 'telescope' flags listed and lines matching either of those
above. The data selection is equivalent to a combination of :

    find /telescope SMT-F1M-HU
    find /telescope SMT-F1M-VU
    find /line N2HP(3-2)
    find /line N2H+(3-2)

ALL of the data matching those criteria will be included in an ObsBlock.
They will then be accessible through the ObsBlock's speclist attribute,
or just by indexing the ObsBlock directly.

```
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Generates a 2D map from the data cube using the specified estimator and enables interactive features.

The map is created by reducing the 3D cube along the spectral axis (using `makeplane`) and then displayed using either `APLpy` (if available and requested) or standard `matplotlib.imshow`.

Interactive Features:

    - **Press 'r'**: Sets the radius of the circle (after center is set with 'c').

makeplane(estimator=np.nanmean)
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Creates a 2D plane from the 3D data cube using the specified reduction method.

The `estimator` parameter controls how the cube is collapsed along the spectral axis:

    - **Function (e.g., `np.mean`, `np.max`)**: Applies the function along axis 0 (spectral).
    - **'max'**: Equivalent to `np.max(cube, axis=0)`.

    - **int**: Index into the `.parcube` attribute (if available), e.g., for moment maps or model parameters.
    - **slice**: Slices the cube along the spectral axis (e.g., `slice(10,20)`).

Raises:

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
Handles user interaction events (mouse clicks, key presses) to extract and plot spectra.

Depending on the event type and button/key used, it:
```

Cubes

Pyspeckit can do a few things with spectral cubes. The most interesting
is the spectral line fitting.

~pyspeckit.cubes.SpectralCube.Cube objects have a
~pyspeckit.cubes.SpectralCube.Cube.fiteach method that will fit each
spectral line within a cube. It can be made to do this in parallel with
the multicore option.

As of version 0.16, pyspeckit cubes can be read from SpectralCube
objects:

    >>> pcube = pyspeckit.Cube(cube=mySpectralCube)

Otherwise, they can be created from FITS cubes on disk:

    >>> pcube = pyspeckit.Cube(filename="mycube.fits")

or from arrays:

    >>> mycube = np.random.randn(250,50,50)
    >>> myxaxis = np.linspace(-100,100,250)

```
-------------

.. automethod:: BaseUser.get_readable
   :noindex:
   Returns a readable representation of the user, using the username.

.. automethod:: BaseUser._validate_password
   :noindex:
   Validates a raw password against minimum and maximum length requirements. Raises `ValueError` if invalid.

.. automethod:: BaseUser.update_password
   :async:
   Asynchronously updates a user's password. Accepts either a user ID or username. The password is automatically hashed before storage.

.. automethod:: BaseUser.update_password_sync
   :noindex:
   Synchronous version of `update_password`.

.. automethod:: BaseUser.hash_password
   :noindex:
   Hashes a raw password using PBKDF2-SHA256. Uses a random salt and default iteration count (600,000) unless overridden.

.. automethod:: BaseUser.login
   :async:

-----------------

Passwords are hashed using PBKDF2-SHA256 with the following defaults:

- **Iteration count**: 600,000 (aligned with OWASP recommendations)
- **Salt**: 16-byte random hex string generated per password
- **Minimum length**: 6 characters
- **Maximum length**: 128 characters

Raw passwords are never stored. Any attempt to set a plain-text password (e.g., via `__setattr__`) is automatically converted to a hashed format.

- The model integrates with Piccolo's async/sync execution model via `run_sync` where needed.
```

BaseUser

BaseUser is a Table you can use to store and authenticate your users.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Creating the Table

Run the migrations:

    piccolo migrations forwards user

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Commands

The app comes with some useful commands.

create

Creates a new user. It presents an interactive prompt, asking for the
username, password etc.

    piccolo user create

If you'd prefer to create a user without the interactive prompt (perhaps
in a script), you can pass all of the arguments in as follows:

    piccolo user create --username=bob --password=bob123 --email=foo@bar.com  --is_admin=t --is_superuser=t --is_active=t

Warning

If you choose this approach then be careful, as the password will be in
the shell's history.

change_password

Change a user's password.

    piccolo user change_password

change_permissions

Change a user's permissions. The options are --admin, --superuser and
--active, which change the corresponding attributes on BaseUser.

For example:

    piccolo user change_permissions some_user --active=true

The Piccolo Admin<PiccoloAdmin> uses these attributes to control who can
login and what they can do.

-   active and admin - must be true for a user to be able to login.
-   superuser - must be true for a user to be able to change other
    user's passwords.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Within your code

create_user / create_user_sync

To create a new user:

    # From within a coroutine:
    await BaseUser.create_user(username="bob", password="abc123", active=True)

    # When not in an event loop:
    BaseUser.create_user_sync(username="bob", password="abc123", active=True)

It saves the user in the database, and returns the created BaseUser
instance.

Note

It is preferable to use this rather than instantiating and saving
BaseUser directly, as we add additional validation.

login / login_sync

To check a user's credentials, do the following:

    from piccolo.apps.user.tables import BaseUser

    # From within a coroutine:
    >>> await BaseUser.login(username="bob", password="abc123")
    1

    # When not in an event loop:
    >>> BaseUser.login_sync(username="bob", password="abc123")
    1

If the login is successful, the user's id is returned, otherwise None is
returned.

update_password / update_password_sync

To change a user's password:

    # From within a coroutine:
    await BaseUser.update_password(username="bob", password="abc123")

    # When not in an event loop:
    BaseUser.update_password_sync(username="bob", password="abc123")

Warning

Don't use bulk updates for passwords - use update_password /
update_password_sync, and they'll correctly hash the password.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Limits

The maximum password length allowed is 128 characters. This should be
sufficiently long for most use cases.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Extending BaseUser

If you want to extend BaseUser with additional fields, we recommend
creating a Profile table with a ForeignKey to BaseUser, which can
include any custom fields.

    from piccolo.apps.user.tables import BaseUser
    from piccolo.columns import ForeignKey, Text, Varchar
    from piccolo.table import Table

    class Profile(Table):
        custom_user = ForeignKey(BaseUser)
        phone_number = Varchar()
        bio = Text()

Alternatively, you can copy the entire user app into your project, and
customise it to fit your needs.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

CockroachEngine
===============

The ``CockroachEngine`` class is an extension of the :class:`PostgresEngine <piccolo.engine.postgres.PostgresEngine>` designed specifically for use with CockroachDB. It inherits most of its functionality from the PostgreSQL engine but includes minor adjustments to better support CockroachDB-specific behaviors and requirements.

This engine allows Piccolo to interface with CockroachDB clusters, enabling schema management, query execution, and integration with Piccolo's ORM features.

Class Definition
----------------

.. autoclass:: piccolo.engine.cockroach.CockroachEngine
   :members:
   :show-inheritance:

Initialization
--------------

.. automethod:: piccolo.engine.cockroach.CockroachEngine.__init__

The ``CockroachEngine`` constructor accepts the following parameters:

- ``config`` (dict): A dictionary containing the database connection settings. Expected keys include ``host``, ``port``, ``database``, ``user``, and ``password``.
- ``extensions`` (Sequence[str]): Optional list of Piccolo extensions to load.
- ``log_queries`` (bool): If ``True``, all generated SQL queries will be logged.
- ``log_responses`` (bool): If ``True``, responses from the database (e.g. query results) will be logged.
- ``extra_nodes`` (Dict[str, CockroachEngine]): A dictionary of read replicas or additional cluster nodes for advanced routing.

Database Preparation
--------------------

.. automethod:: piccolo.engine.cockroach.CockroachEngine.prep_database

Before using the database, ``prep_database`` attempts to enable the experimental ``ALTER COLUMN TYPE`` setting in CockroachDB, which is required for certain schema modification operations. If the connected user lacks sufficient privileges, a warning is issued, but the engine continues to function with limited capabilities.

Version Compatibility
---------------------

- ``engine_type``: ``"cockroach"``
- ``min_version_number``: ``0`` — version checking is currently disabled due to differences in CockroachDB's versioning scheme compared to PostgreSQL.

Privilege Requirements
----------------------

For full functionality, the database user should have permissions to set cluster-level settings. Specifically, the ability to run:

.. code-block:: sql

   SET CLUSTER SETTING sql.defaults.experimental_alter_column_type.enabled = true;

If this permission is missing, a medium-level warning is displayed, indicating that some operations may not behave as expected.

Usage Example
-------------

.. code-block:: python

   from piccolo.engine.cockroach import CockroachEngine

   DB = CockroachEngine(
       config={
           "host": "localhost",
           "port": 26257,
           "database": "mydb",
           "user": "root",
           "password": "",
       },
       log_queries=True,
   )

   # Prepare the database
   await DB.prep_database()

This engine can then be used throughout your Piccolo application as the default database engine.

config

The config dictionary is passed directly to the underlying database
adapter, asyncpg. See the asyncpg docs to learn more.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Connection pool

To use a connection pool, you need to first initialise it. The best
place to do this is in the startup event handler of whichever web
framework you are using.

Here's an example using Starlette. Notice that we also close the
connection pool in the shutdown event handler.

    from piccolo.engine import engine_finder
    from starlette.applications import Starlette


    app = Starlette()


    @app.on_event('startup')
    async def open_database_connection_pool():
        engine = engine_finder()
        await engine.start_connection_pool()


    @app.on_event('shutdown')
    async def close_database_connection_pool():
        engine = engine_finder()
        await engine.close_connection_pool()

Hint

Using a connection pool helps with performance, since connections are
reused instead of being created for each query.

Once a connection pool has been started, the engine will use it for
making queries.

Hint

If you're running several instances of an app on the same server, you
may prefer an external connection pooler - like pgbouncer.

Configuration

The connection pool uses the same configuration as your engine. You can
also pass in additional parameters, which are passed to the underlying
database adapter. Here's an example:

    # To increase the number of connections available:
    await engine.start_connection_pool(max_size=20)

```rst
The `piccolo_apps` module provides core functionality for managing Piccolo applications, including app configuration, table discovery, migration handling, and project-wide registry management. Automatically discovers `Table` subclasses from specified modules, optionally filtering by tags or excluding imported tables.

   from piccolo.apps import table_finder

   tables = table_finder(['blog.tables', 'forum.tables'])

   tagged_tables = table_finder(
       modules=['blog.tables'],
       include_tags=['public', 'featured']

   filtered_tables = table_finder(
       modules=['blog.tables'],
       exclude_tags=['internal']
```

Piccolo Apps

By leveraging Piccolo apps you can:

-   Modularise your code.
-   Share your apps with other Piccolo users.
-   Unlock some useful functionality like auto migrations.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Creating an app

Run the following command within your project:

    piccolo app new my_app

Where my_app is your new app's name. This will create a folder like
this:

    my_app/
        __init__.py
        piccolo_app.py
        piccolo_migrations/
            __init__.py
        tables.py

It's important to register your new app with the APP_REGISTRY in
piccolo_conf.py.

    # piccolo_conf.py
    APP_REGISTRY = AppRegistry(apps=['my_app.piccolo_app'])

Anytime you invoke the piccolo command, you will now be able to perform
operations on your app, such as Migrations.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

AppConfig

Inside your app's piccolo_app.py file is an AppConfig instance. This is
how you customise your app's settings.

    # piccolo_app.py
    import os

    from piccolo.conf.apps import AppConfig
    from .tables import (
        Author,
        Post,
        Category,
        CategoryToPost,
    )


    CURRENT_DIRECTORY = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))


    APP_CONFIG = AppConfig(
        app_name='blog',
        migrations_folder_path=os.path.join(
            CURRENT_DIRECTORY,
            'piccolo_migrations'
        ),
        table_classes=[Author, Post, Category, CategoryToPost],
        migration_dependencies=[],
        commands=[]
    )

app_name

This is used to identify your app, when using the piccolo CLI, for
example:

    piccolo migrations forwards blog

migrations_folder_path

Specifies where your app's migrations are stored. By default, a folder
called piccolo_migrations is used.

table_classes

Use this to register your app's Table subclasses. This is important for
auto migrations <Migrations>.

You can register them manually (see the example above), or can use
table_finder <TableFinder>.

migration_dependencies

Used to specify other Piccolo apps whose migrations need to be run
before the current app's migrations.

commands

You can register functions and coroutines, which are automatically added
to the piccolo CLI.

The targ library is used under the hood. It makes it really easy to
write command lines tools - just use type annotations and docstrings.
Here's an example:

    def say_hello(name: str):
        """
        Say hello.

        :param name:
            The person to greet.

        """
        print("hello,", name)

We then register it with the AppConfig.

    # piccolo_app.py

    APP_CONFIG = AppConfig(
        # ...
        commands=[say_hello]
    )

And from the command line:

    >>> piccolo my_app say_hello bob
    hello, bob

If the code contains an error to see more details in the output add a
--trace flag to the command line.

    >>> piccolo my_app say_hello bob --trace

By convention, store the command definitions in a commands folder in
your app.

    my_app/
        __init__.py
        piccolo_app.py
        commands/
            __init__.py
            say_hello.py

Piccolo itself is bundled with several apps - have a look at the source
code for inspiration.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

table_finder

Instead of manually registering Table subclasses, you can use
table_finder to automatically import any Table subclasses from a given
list of modules.

    from piccolo.conf.apps import table_finder

    APP_CONFIG = AppConfig(
        app_name='blog',
        migrations_folder_path=os.path.join(
            CURRENT_DIRECTORY,
            'piccolo_migrations'
        ),
        table_classes=table_finder(modules=['blog.tables']),
        migration_dependencies=[],
        commands=[]
    )

The module path should be from the root of the project (the same
directory as your piccolo_conf.py file, rather than a relative path).

You can filter the Table subclasses returned using tags <TableTags>.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Sharing Apps

By breaking up your project into apps, the project becomes more
maintainable. You can also share these apps between projects, and they
can even be installed using pip.

```rst
    - ``get_table_classes(app_name)``: Returns all table classes registered with the app.
    - ``get_table_with_name(app_name, table_class_name)``: Returns a specific table class by name.

Finder
~~~~~~
A utility class for locating and loading Piccolo configuration and app modules across the project.

Features:
    - Resolves the main ``piccolo_conf`` module, respecting the ``PICCOLO_CONF`` environment variable.
    - Loads the database engine and app registry.
    - Recursively imports all app modules, including dependencies, in correct order.
    - Supports diagnostic mode to help debug import issues.

Methods:
    - ``get_piccolo_conf_module()``: Imports and returns the ``piccolo_conf`` module.
    - ``get_engine()``: Returns the configured database engine (e.g., PostgreSQL or SQLite).
    - ``get_app_registry()``: Returns the global ``AppRegistry`` instance.
    - ``get_app_modules()``: Returns a deduplicated list of all ``piccolo_app.py`` modules.
    - ``get_app_names()``: Returns a list of app names, optionally sorted by migration dependencies (ensuring dependent apps come later).

table_finder
~~~~~~~~~~~~
Dynamically discovers ``Table`` subclasses from specified modules, optionally filtered by tags or module ownership.

Useful for automatically registering tables without manually listing them.

Arguments:
    - ``modules`` (Sequence[str]): Module paths to search (e.g., ``['blog.tables']``).
    - ``include_tags`` (Sequence[str]): Only include tables with at least one of these tags. Use ``['__all__']`` to include all.
    - ``exclude_tags`` (Sequence[str]): Exclude tables with any of these tags (takes precedence over ``include_tags``).
    - ``exclude_imported`` (bool): If ``True``, only includes tables defined directly in the module, not imported from elsewhere.

Returns:
    List of ``Table`` subclasses matching the criteria.

Example:
    .. code-block:: python

        from piccolo.utils import table_finder

        TABLE_CLASSES = table_finder(
            modules=['blog.tables', 'forum.tables'],
            include_tags=['web'],
            exclude_tags=['experimental']
        )

MigrationModule
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
A type stub for migration modules (e.g., ``migrations/001_forward.py``). Each migration module must define:
    - ``ID`` (str): A unique identifier for the migration.
    - ``VERSION`` (str): The version string.
    - ``DESCRIPTION`` (str): Human-readable description.
    - ``forwards()`` (async function): Contains the migration logic.

PiccoloAppModule
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
A type stub representing a ``piccolo_app.py`` module, which must define an ``APP_CONFIG`` attribute of type ``AppConfig``.

PiccoloConfModule
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
A type stub for the ``piccolo_conf.py`` module, which must define:
    - ``DB``: An instance of a Piccolo ``Engine`` (e.g., ``PostgresEngine``).
    - ``APP_REGISTRY``: An instance of ``AppRegistry``.

Utilities
---------
- ``Command``: A dataclass wrapper for CLI commands, allowing aliases and custom callables.
- ``TopologicalSorter``: Used internally to sort apps by migration dependencies.
- Environment Variable: ``PICCOLO_CONF`` can be set to override the default ``piccolo_conf`` module location.

Usage in Projects
-----------------
This module is used internally by Piccolo's CLI (e.g., ``piccolo migrations generate``, ``piccolo run``) to:
    - Discover all tables and apps.
    - Determine migration order.
    - Execute app-specific commands.
    - Connect to the correct database engine.

It forms the backbone of Piccolo’s plugin-style app architecture, enabling modular, reusable components.

- ``piccolo_cli``: For command-line interface integration.
```

```rst
==================
Postgres Engine
==================

The ``PostgresEngine`` class is the primary interface for connecting to and interacting with a PostgreSQL database in Piccolo. It provides support for asynchronous queries, connection pooling, transactions, savepoints, and integration with read replicas.

It uses `asyncpg <https://magicstack.github.io/asyncpg/current/>`_ under the hood for high-performance database access.

------------------
Engine Initialization
------------------

To connect to a PostgreSQL database, instantiate the ``PostgresEngine`` with a config dictionary containing connection parameters:

.. code-block:: python

    from piccolo.engine.postgres import PostgresEngine

    DB = PostgresEngine(
        config={
            "database": "my_db",
            "user": "piccolo",
            "password": "piccolo123",
            "host": "localhost",
            "port": 5432,
        }
    )

The ``config`` dictionary is passed directly to ``asyncpg.connect()``, so all standard connection arguments are supported.

------------------
Configuration Options
------------------

``PostgresEngine`` supports several optional parameters:

- ``extensions`` (default: ``("uuid-ossp",)``): A sequence of PostgreSQL extensions to create when the engine starts. Set to an empty tuple if using a read-only database.
- ``log_queries`` (default: ``False``): If ``True``, all SQL and DDL statements are printed before execution.
- ``log_responses`` (default: ``True``): If ``True``, raw query responses are printed for debugging.
- ``extra_nodes``: A mapping of node names to additional ``PostgresEngine`` instances (e.g., for read replicas).

Example with read replica:

.. code-block:: python

    DB = PostgresEngine(
        config={'database': 'main_db'},
        extra_nodes={
            'read_replica_1': PostgresEngine(
                config={
                    'database': 'main_db',
                    'host': 'read_replica.my_db.com',
                    'user': 'readonly_user',
                    'password': 'readonly_pass'
                },
                extensions=()  # Read-only, so no extensions
            )
        }
    )

You can then run queries on a specific node:

.. code-block:: python

    await MyTable.select().run(node="read_replica_1")

------------------
Connection Pooling
------------------

For improved performance in production, use connection pooling:

.. code-block:: python

    await DB.start_connection_pool()

This creates an internal ``asyncpg.Pool``. You can pass additional arguments to ``start_connection_pool()``, which are merged with the base config.

To close the pool:

.. code-block:: python

    await DB.close_connection_pool()

There are also deprecated aliases ``start_connnection_pool`` and ``close_connnection_pool`` (with a typo) for backward compatibility.

------------------
Transactions
------------------

Piccolo supports async context manager-based transactions:

.. code-block:: python

    async with DB.transaction():
        await Band.insert(
            Band(name="Pythonistas")
        )
        await Venue.insert(
            Venue(name="The Shell")
        )
        await Concert.insert(
            Concert(band=1, venue=1)
        )

If an exception occurs, the transaction is automatically rolled back. Otherwise, it is committed.

Nested Transactions
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

By default, nested transaction blocks are allowed and treated as a no-op:

.. code-block:: python

    async with DB.transaction():
        async with DB.transaction():  # This does nothing
            pass

To disallow nesting and raise an error instead:

.. code-block:: python

    async with DB.transaction(allow_nested=False):
        async with DB.transaction():  # Raises TransactionError
            pass

Manual Transaction Control
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

You can also use the ``atomic()`` method to build up a transaction programmatically:

.. code-block:: python

    transaction = DB.atomic()
    transaction.add(Band.insert(Band(name="Pythonistas")))
    transaction.add(Venue.insert(Venue(name="The Shell")))

    await transaction.run()  # Run async
    transaction.run_sync()   # Run synchronously

------------------
Savepoints
------------------

Within a transaction, you can create savepoints to allow partial rollbacks:

.. code-block:: python

    async with DB.transaction() as tx:
        await Band.insert(Band(name="Before Savepoint"))

        savepoint = await tx.savepoint()
        await Band.insert(Band(name="After Savepoint"))

        await savepoint.rollback_to()  # Rolls back to savepoint
        # Only "Before Savepoint" remains

        # Or release the savepoint
        await savepoint.release()

You can also name savepoints:

.. code-block:: python

    savepoint = await tx.savepoint("my_savepoint")
    await tx.rollback_to("my_savepoint")

------------------
Batched Queries
------------------

For large result sets, use ``batch()`` to fetch results in chunks:

.. code-block:: python

    async for batch in DB.batch(MyTable.select(), batch_size=200):
        for row in batch:
            print(row)

This returns an async iterator that yields lists of dictionaries, each of size up to ``batch_size``.

------------------
Database Version
------------------

You can retrieve the PostgreSQL server version:

.. code-block:: python

    version = await DB.get_version()  # e.g. 14.5
    version_sync = DB.get_version_sync()  # Synchronous version

This is useful for conditional logic based on database capabilities.

------------------
Extension Management
------------------

On startup, the engine attempts to create the specified extensions (e.g., ``uuid-ossp``). If the user lacks privileges, a warning is shown but execution continues.

To disable extension creation (e.g., for read-only databases), set ``extensions=()``.

------------------
Internal Classes
------------------

AsyncBatch
~~~~~~~~~~

An async iterator for processing query results in batches. Used internally by ``DB.batch()``.

Atomic
~~~~~~

Wraps multiple queries into a single transaction. Used by ``DB.atomic()``.

Savepoint
~~~~~~~~~

Represents a named savepoint within a transaction. Supports ``rollback_to()`` and ``release()``.

PostgresTransaction
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Manages the lifecycle of a PostgreSQL transaction. Handles connection acquisition, context management, and cleanup. Uses Python's ``contextvars`` to track the current transaction per async task.

------------------
Error Handling
------------------

- ``TransactionError``: Raised when attempting to start a nested transaction with ``allow_nested=False``.
- Warnings are issued via ``colored_warning`` for issues like connection failures or missing extensions.

------------------
Synchronous Support
------------------

While the engine is async-first, synchronous versions of key methods are available via ``run_sync()``:

- ``get_version_sync()``
- ``run_sync()`` on atomic transactions

This allows integration with synchronous codebases or testing environments.

------------------
Summary
------------------

The ``PostgresEngine`` provides a full-featured, async-ready interface to PostgreSQL with support for:

- Connection pooling
- Transactions and savepoints
- Read replicas
- Query logging
- Extension management
- Batched result processing

It integrates seamlessly with the rest of the Piccolo ORM and is the recommended engine for PostgreSQL users.
```

Connection pool

To use a connection pool, you need to first initialise it. The best
place to do this is in the startup event handler of whichever web
framework you are using.

Here's an example using Starlette. Notice that we also close the
connection pool in the shutdown event handler.

    from piccolo.engine import engine_finder
    from starlette.applications import Starlette


    app = Starlette()


    @app.on_event('startup')
    async def open_database_connection_pool():
        engine = engine_finder()
        await engine.start_connection_pool()


    @app.on_event('shutdown')
    async def close_database_connection_pool():
        engine = engine_finder()
        await engine.close_connection_pool()

Hint

Using a connection pool helps with performance, since connections are
reused instead of being created for each query.

Once a connection pool has been started, the engine will use it for
making queries.

Hint

If you're running several instances of an app on the same server, you
may prefer an external connection pooler - like pgbouncer.

Configuration

The connection pool uses the same configuration as your engine. You can
also pass in additional parameters, which are passed to the underlying
database adapter. Here's an example:

    # To increase the number of connections available:
    await engine.start_connection_pool(max_size=20)

```rst
Running Migrations
==================

This module provides functionality for managing database migrations in Piccolo apps, including running migrations forwards and backwards, checking migration status, and previewing migration SQL.

Key Features
------------

- **Run migrations forwards or backwards** up to a specific migration ID.
- **Check the status** of all migrations (which have run and which haven't).
- Support for **preview mode**, which shows the SQL without applying changes.
- Option to **auto-agree** to prompts for use in scripts.
- Ability to **clean up** migration files after reversing them.

Running Migrations Forwards
---------------------------

To apply pending migrations, use the ``forwards`` function:

.. autofunction:: forwards

This will run migrations that haven't been applied yet. You can specify:

- ``app_name``: The app to migrate (use ``'all'`` for all apps).
- ``migration_id``: Run up to a specific migration. Use ``'all'`` to run all pending, or ``'1'`` to run just the next one.
- ``fake``: If ``True``, marks migrations as run without actually applying them.
- ``preview``: If ``True``, prints the SQL but doesn't execute it.

Reversing Migrations
--------------------

To undo previously applied migrations, use the ``backwards`` function:

.. autofunction:: backwards

This allows you to roll back migrations. Parameters include:

- ``app_name``: App to reverse migrations for (``'all'`` reverses all apps).
- ``migration_id``: Reverse up to this migration. Use ``'all'`` to reverse all, or ``'1'`` to reverse only the most recent.
- ``auto_agree``: Bypass confirmation prompts.
- ``clean``: If ``True``, deletes migration files from disk after reversal.
- ``preview``: Show SQL without executing.

Checking Migration Status
-------------------------

To list all migrations and their status (whether they've been applied), use:

.. autofunction:: check

This displays a table showing:

- App name
- Migration ID
- Description
- Whether the migration has been run

The output helps identify which migrations are pending and which have already been applied.

Migration Status Report
-----------------------

The ``CheckMigrationManager`` returns structured status information via ``MigrationStatus``:

.. autoclass:: MigrationStatus
   :members:

Utility Functions
-----------------

- ``run_forwards()``: Programmatic interface to run migrations (useful in tests).
- ``run_backwards()``: Programmatic interface to reverse migrations.

These return a ``MigrationResult`` object indicating success or failure.

Preview Mode
------------

Both forward and backward operations support ``preview=True``, which outputs the raw SQL that would be executed, without making any changes to the database. This is useful for auditing or debugging migration logic.

Automatic Mode
--------------

Use ``auto_agree=True`` to skip interactive prompts. This is essential for automated deployment scripts where user input isn't possible.

Cleanup Mode
------------

When reversing migrations with ``clean=True``, the corresponding migration Python files are deleted from the filesystem after reversal. Use with caution in production environments.

Error Handling
--------------

All operations return a ``MigrationResult(success: bool, message: str)``. If a migration fails, the function exits with status code 1, making it suitable for use in CI/CD pipelines.

Usage Examples
--------------

Run all pending migrations for an app:

.. code-block:: python

   await forwards(app_name="blog")

Reverse the last migration with confirmation:

.. code-block:: python

   await backwards(app_name="blog", migration_id="1")

Preview the SQL for reversing all migrations:

.. code-block:: python

   await backwards(app_name="blog", migration_id="all", preview=True, auto_agree=True)

Check status of all migrations:

.. code-block:: python

   await check(app_name="all")
```

```rst
Using SQLite and asyncio Effectively with Piccolo
=================================================

Piccolo provides a robust and efficient SQLite engine that integrates seamlessly with both synchronous and asynchronous Python code. This document explains how to use SQLite effectively in combination with `asyncio`, leveraging Piccolo's features for transactions, type handling, batching, and more.

Type Conversion and Data Consistency
------------------------------------

SQLite has limited native support for certain data types compared to other databases like PostgreSQL. To ensure consistent behavior across different database backends, Piccolo registers custom adapters and converters for Python types such as `datetime`, `UUID`, `Decimal`, and `list`.

Incoming Data (Adapters)
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

When inserting data into SQLite, Piccolo automatically converts the following types:

- :py:class:`decimal.Decimal` → converted to float
- :py:class:`uuid.UUID` → converted to string
- :py:class:`datetime.time` → ISO format string
- :py:class:`datetime.date` → ISO format string
- :py:class:`datetime.datetime` → string; if timezone-aware, converted to UTC first
- :py:class:`datetime.timedelta` → total seconds as float
- :py:class:`list` → JSON-encoded string (only supports str, int, float elements)

Outgoing Data (Converters)
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

When retrieving data from SQLite, Piccolo restores values to their original Python types using registered converters:

- ``Numeric`` → :py:class:`decimal.Decimal`
- ``Integer`` → :py:class:`int`
- ``UUID`` → :py:class:`uuid.UUID`
- ``Date`` → :py:class:`datetime.date`
- ``Time`` → :py:class:`datetime.time`
- ``Seconds`` → :py:class:`datetime.timedelta`
- ``Boolean`` → :py:class:`bool` (stored as "1" or "0")
- ``Timestamp`` / ``Timestamptz`` → :py:class:`datetime.datetime` (UTC for timestamptz)
- ``Array`` → deserialized from JSON back to :py:class:`list`
- ``M2M`` → comma-separated string converted to list of strings

These conversions ensure that your application logic works consistently regardless of the underlying database.

Async Support with aiosqlite
----------------------------

Piccolo uses `aiosqlite` under the hood to provide full async support for SQLite operations. The integration is lazy-loaded, meaning `aiosqlite` is only imported when needed.

To run queries asynchronously:

.. code-block:: python

    async with engine.transaction():
        await Band.select().run()

All query methods (e.g., `.run()`) are awaitable and work natively in async contexts.

Transactions
------------

SQLite supports transactions via the `BEGIN`, `COMMIT`, and `ROLLBACK` statements. Piccolo wraps this functionality in a clean, context-manager-based API.

Transaction Types
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

You can specify the transaction type when starting a transaction:

- ``TransactionType.deferred`` (default): Locks the database only when needed; best for read-heavy workloads.
- ``TransactionType.immediate``: Acquires a reserved lock immediately; recommended for write operations to avoid lock contention.
- ``TransactionType.exclusive``: Prevents other connections from reading or writing during the transaction.

Example usage:

.. code-block:: python

    async with engine.transaction(transaction_type=TransactionType.immediate):
        await Band.insert(
            Band(name="Pythonistas", popularity=1000)
        ).run()

Nested Transactions and Savepoints
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

SQLite does not support true nested transactions, but Piccolo emulates nesting using **savepoints** when ``allow_nested=True`` (the default).

You can manually create and manage savepoints:

.. code-block:: python

    async with engine.transaction() as tx:
        sp = await tx.savepoint()
        try:
            await Band.insert(Band(name="Invalid")).run()
        except Exception:
            await sp.rollback_to()  # Roll back to savepoint
        await sp.release()  # Release savepoint

If an exception occurs within a transaction block, it will be automatically rolled back unless already committed or rolled back manually.

Atomic Query Execution
----------------------

The `Atomic` class allows you to group multiple queries into a single transaction and execute them together.

.. code-block:: python

    transaction = engine.atomic()
    transaction.add(Band.insert(Band(name="Band A")))
    transaction.add(Musician.insert(Musician(name="Alice")))

    await transaction.run()  # Runs all queries in one transaction

This is useful for ensuring data consistency across multiple operations.

Batched Query Results
---------------------

For large result sets, Piccolo provides an async batch iterator to stream results in chunks, reducing memory usage.

.. code-block:: python

    batch = await Band.select().batch(batch_size=100)

    async for rows in batch:
        for row in rows:
            print(row)

The `AsyncBatch` class handles pagination and result processing transparently.

Connection Management
---------------------

Piccolo manages SQLite connections efficiently using context managers and connection pooling patterns. Connections are automatically opened and closed within transaction or query contexts.

The engine accepts standard SQLite connection parameters via `connection_kwargs`, such as:

- ``timeout``: How long to wait before raising an OperationalError when the database is locked (recommended for high-concurrency apps).
- ``detect_types``: Enabled by default to support type converters.

Example:

.. code-block:: python

    engine = SQLiteEngine(
        path="myapp.db",
        log_queries=True,
        timeout=10.0
    )

Logging
-------

Enable logging to debug SQL queries and responses:

- ``log_queries=True``: Prints all SQL statements before execution.
- ``log_responses=True``: Prints raw responses from the database.

Useful during development and troubleshooting.

Synchronous Compatibility
-------------------------

All async functionality can be used synchronously via `run_sync()`:

.. code-block:: python

    engine.atomic().add(Band.create_table()).run_sync()

This makes it easy to integrate Piccolo into existing sync codebases.

Best Practices
--------------

1. **Use Transactions for Related Operations**: Wrap related inserts, updates, or deletes in a transaction to maintain data integrity.
2. **Set a Timeout**: Always set a `timeout` in `connection_kwargs` to prevent indefinite blocking under high load.
3. **Prefer Immediate Transactions for Writes**: Use `TransactionType.immediate` when performing write operations to reduce the chance of lock errors.
4. **Use Batching for Large Datasets**: When querying large tables, use `.batch()` to avoid memory overflow.
5. **Enable Logging in Development**: Use `log_queries=True` during development to inspect generated SQL.

Conclusion
----------

Piccolo’s SQLite engine offers a powerful, asyncio-native interface while maintaining compatibility with synchronous code. With automatic type conversion, transaction management, savepoints, and efficient batching, it enables you to build scalable and reliable applications using SQLite as your database backend.
```

Using SQLite and asyncio effectively

When using Piccolo with SQLite, there are some best practices to follow.

asyncio => lots of connections

With asyncio, we can potentially open lots of database connections, and
attempt to perform concurrent database writes.

SQLite doesn't support such concurrent behavior as effectively as
Postgres, so we need to be careful.

One write at a time

SQLite can easily support lots of transactions concurrently if they are
reading, but only one write can be performed at a time.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

Transactions

SQLite has several transaction types, as specified by Piccolo's
TransactionType enum:

piccolo.engine.sqlite

TransactionType

Which to use?

When creating a transaction, Piccolo uses DEFERRED by default (to be
consistent with SQLite).

This means that the first SQL query executed within the transaction
determines whether it's a READ or WRITE:

-   READ - if the first query is a SELECT
-   WRITE - if the first query is something like an INSERT / UPDATE /
    DELETE

If a transaction starts off with a SELECT, but then tries to perform an
INSERT / UPDATE / DELETE, SQLite tries to 'promote' the transaction so
it can write.

The problem is, if multiple concurrent connections try doing this at the
same time, SQLite will return a database locked error.

So if you're creating a transaction which you know will perform writes,
then create an IMMEDIATE transaction:

    from piccolo.engine.sqlite import TransactionType

    async with Band._meta.db.transaction(
        transaction_type=TransactionType.immediate
    ):
        # We perform a SELECT first, but as it's an IMMEDIATE transaction,
        # we can later perform writes without getting a database locked
        # error.
        if not await Band.exists().where(Band.name == 'Pythonistas'):
            await Band.objects().create(name="Pythonistas")

Multiple IMMEDIATE transactions can exist concurrently - SQLite uses a
lock to make sure only one of them writes at a time.

If your transaction will just be performing SELECT queries, then just
use the default DEFERRED transactions - you will get improved
performance, as no locking is involved:

    async with Band._meta.db.transaction():
        bands = await Band.select()
        managers = await Manager.select()

------------------------------------------------------------------------

timeout

It's recommended to specify the timeout argument in
SQLiteEngine <piccolo.engine.sqlite.SQLiteEngine>.

    DB = SQLiteEngine(timeout=60)

Imagine you have a web app, and each endpoint creates a transaction
which runs multiple queries. With SQLite, only a single write operation
can happen at a time, so if several connections are open, they may be
queued for a while.

By increasing timeout it means that queries are less likely to timeout.

To find out more about timeout see the Python
sqlite3 docs <sqlite3.connect>.

Augmentations
=============

This module provides a collection of image augmentation functions designed for use with automatic augmentation policies such as **AutoAugment**, **RandAugment**, and **TrivialAugmentWide**. All augmentations are implemented using NVIDIA DALI operators for high-performance data loading and preprocessing.

Each augmentation is decorated with ``@augmentation``, which enables automatic parameter computation based on magnitude bins. When used in a policy, the user provides:

- A batch of input data (positional argument)
- ``magnitude_bin``: index selecting the strength from a discretized range
- ``num_magnitude_bins``: total number of discrete magnitude levels

The actual parameter applied to the transformation is computed as:

.. math::

   \text{param} = \text{mag\_to\_param}\left(\text{magnitudes}[magnitude\_bin] \times (-1)^{\text{random\_sign}}\right)

where ``magnitudes`` is linearly spaced between the specified ``mag_range[0]`` and ``mag_range[1]``.

All augmentations support optional arguments:

- ``fill_value``: value used to fill areas outside the transformed image (default: 128)
- ``interp_type``: interpolation method (e.g., ``types.INTERP_LINEAR``, ``types.INTERP_NN``, etc.)

Below is a list of available augmentations.

Customization
-------------

The augmentations are highly customizable via the ``augmentation`` decorator. You can override any of the default parameters such as ``mag_range``, ``randomly_negate``, or ``mag_to_param``.

For example, to increase the shear magnitude range:

.. code-block:: python

   my_shear_x = shear_x.augmentation(mag_range=(0, 0.5))

This creates a new version of ``shear_x`` with an extended magnitude range while preserving all other behavior.

See the :ref:`auto_augment_policy` module for how these augmentations are used in policy construction.

.. _auto-augment-module:

Auto Augment
============

The ``nvidia.dali.auto_aug`` module provides a set of utilities to apply automatic data augmentation policies to image and video data within NVIDIA DALI pipelines. These policies are based on the AutoAugment method introduced in the paper `Learning Data Augmentation Strategies for Deep Learning <https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.09501>`_, which learns optimal augmentation strategies from data.

This module enables users to apply predefined augmentation policies such as those tuned for ImageNet, CIFAR-10, and SVHN, or to define and apply custom policies using a flexible functional API.

Main Functions
--------------

~~~~~~~~~~~~

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

---------------------------

~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Augmentation Policies
---------------------

The module includes several predefined augmentation policies, each designed for specific datasets and use cases:

- **ImageNet Policy**: A full augmentation policy optimized for the ImageNet dataset, containing a diverse set of color, geometric, and pixel-level transformations.
- **Reduced ImageNet Policy**: A simplified version of the ImageNet policy with fewer sub-policies, suitable for faster experimentation.
- **SVHN Policy**: Tailored for the Street View House Numbers (SVHN) dataset, focusing on transformations that preserve digit legibility.
- **Reduced CIFAR-10 Policy**: Designed for the CIFAR-10 dataset with reduced complexity, balancing performance and augmentation strength.

Each policy consists of multiple sub-policies, where each sub-policy defines a sequence of two augmentations (in most cases), along with their respective probabilities and magnitude bins. During execution, one sub-policy is randomly selected per sample, and augmentations are applied conditionally based on their probabilities.

Supported Augmentations
-----------------------

The following augmentations are used within the predefined policies:

- **Color**: Adjusts the color balance of images.
- **Brightness**: Modifies image brightness.
- **Contrast**: Alters image contrast.
- **Sharpness**: Adjusts image sharpness using convolution kernels.
- **Shear (X/Y)**: Applies shear transformation along X or Y axis.
- **Rotate**: Rotates the image by a specified angle.
- **Translate (X/Y)**: Translates the image horizontally or vertically.
- **Posterize**: Reduces the number of bits per color channel.
- **Solarize**: Inverts pixel values above a threshold.
- **SolarizeAdd**: Adds a value to pixels below a threshold.
- **Invert**: Inverts all pixel values.
- **Equalize**: Equalizes the image histogram.
- **AutoContrast**: Maximizes the image contrast by stretching the intensity range.

Usage Notes
-----------

- Input data must be of type ``uint8`` and have layout `HWC` for images or `FHWC` for videos.
- The `shape` argument can be used to make translation magnitudes relative to input dimensions, which is useful when processing variable-sized inputs.
- The `fill_value` parameter controls the padding value used during affine transformations (e.g., translation, rotation). If set to `None`, edge values are repeated (clamped).
- Interpolation type for affine operations can be specified via `interp_type`, supporting `types.INTERP_LINEAR` (default) and `types.INTERP_NN`.

Dependencies
------------

The module requires `NumPy` for internal computations. If NumPy is not installed, an import error will be raised.

Example
-------

.. code-block:: python

    from nvidia.dali import fn
    from nvidia.dali.auto_aug import auto_augment

    # Define a pipeline with AutoAugment
    def define_pipeline():
        images = fn.readers.file(file_root="path/to/images")
        decoded = fn.decoders.image(images, device="cpu")
        augmented = auto_augment(decoded, policy_name="image_net", fill_value=128)
        return augmented

See Also
--------

- :ref:`augmentation-ops` – Built-in DALI augmentation operations.
- :ref:`fn-module` – Functional API for building DALI pipelines.
- `Original AutoAugment Paper <https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.09501>`_ – Research background and methodology.
results.reference:
AutoAugment

AutoAugment, as described in https://arxiv.org/abs/1805.09501, builds
policies out of pairs of augmentations <Augmentation operations> called
subpolicies. Each subpolicy specifies sequence of operations with the
probability of application and the magnitude parameter. When AutoAugment
is used, for each sample a random subpolicy is selected and applied.

To use the predefined policy that was discovered on ImageNet, import and
invoke ~nvidia.dali.auto_aug.auto_augment.auto_augment inside the
pipeline definition, for example:

    from nvidia.dali import pipeline_def
    from nvidia.dali.auto_aug import auto_augment

    @pipeline_def(enable_conditionals=True)
    def training_pipe(data_dir, image_size):

        jpegs, labels = fn.readers.file(file_root=data_dir, ...)
        shapes = fn.peek_image_shape(jpegs)
        images = fn.decoders.image(jpegs, device="mixed", output_type=types.RGB)

        augmented_images = auto_augment.auto_augment(images, shape=shapes)

        resized_images = fn.resize(augmented_images, size=[image_size, image_size])

        return resized_images, labels

Warning

You need to define the pipeline with the
@pipeline_def <nvidia.dali.pipeline_def> decorator and set
enable_conditionals to True to use automatic augmentations.

Refer to this <Building and invoking custom policies> section to read
more about using custom policies.

Invoking predefined AutoAugment policies

To invoke one of the predefined policies use the following functions.

Building and invoking custom policies

DALI's AutoAugment implementation relies on
~nvidia.dali.auto_aug.core.Policy class to define the policies to
execute, which can be invoked within the pipeline using
~nvidia.dali.auto_aug.auto_augment.apply_auto_augment function.

The best way is to wrap your policy creation into a function:

    from nvidia.dali.auto_aug import augmentations
    from nvidia.dali.auto_aug.core import Policy

    def my_custom_policy() -> Policy:
         """
         Creates a simple AutoAugment policy with 3 sub-policies using custom magnitude ranges.
         """

         shear_x = augmentations.shear_x.augmentation((0, 0.5), True)
         shear_y = augmentations.shear_y.augmentation((0, 0.5), True)
         rotate = augmentations.rotate.augmentation((0, 40), True)
         invert = augmentations.invert
         return Policy(
             name="SimplePolicy", num_magnitude_bins=11, sub_policies=[
                 [(shear_x, 0.8, 7), (shear_y, 0.8, 4)],
                 [(invert, 0.4, None), (rotate, 0.6, 8)],
                 [(rotate, 0.6, 7), (shear_y, 0.6, 3)],
             ])

The tuple within the subpolicy definition specifies:

-   the augmentation to use,
-   the probability of applying that augmentation (if this subpolicy is
    selected),
-   the magnitude to be used.

Accessing predefined policies

To obtain the predefined policy definition refer to the following
functions.

.. _rand_augment_module:

RandAugment
===========

The ``rand_augment`` module provides an implementation of the RandAugment policy, introduced in the paper *"RandAugment: Practical automated data augmentation with a reduced search space"* (`arXiv:1909.13719 <https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.13719>`__). This method simplifies automated data augmentation by applying a fixed set of transformations with a randomly selected subset applied per sample, each using a shared magnitude.

The module allows users to apply RandAugment directly using a default suite of augmentations or customize the process by selecting specific operations, excluding unwanted ones, or defining custom augmentation lists.

Main Functions
--------------

.. autofunction:: nvidia.dali.auto_aug.rand_augment.rand_augment

.. autofunction:: nvidia.dali.auto_aug.rand_augment.apply_rand_augment

Augmentation Suites
-------------------

The module includes two predefined augmentation suites that differ in how the magnitude bins map to operation strength.

.. autofunction:: nvidia.dali.auto_aug.rand_augment.get_rand_augment_suite

.. autofunction:: nvidia.dali.auto_aug.rand_augment.get_rand_augment_non_monotonic_suite

Default Augmentation Suite
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

The default suite returned by :func:`get_rand_augment_suite` includes the following operations:

- ``translate_x``, ``translate_y`` – translation along X and Y axes
- ``shear_x``, ``shear_y`` – shearing transformations
- ``rotate`` – rotation
- ``brightness``, ``contrast``, ``color``, ``sharpness`` – enhancement operations with increasing strength
- ``posterize`` – reduces the number of bits per channel (strength increases with magnitude)
- ``solarize`` – inverts pixels above a threshold (strength increases as threshold decreases)
- ``equalize`` – equalizes histogram of image
- ``auto_contrast`` – maximizes contrast by stretching intensity range
- ``identity`` – no-op operation

The strength of most operations increases monotonically with the magnitude bin. This behavior is controlled via the ``monotonic_mag`` parameter in :func:`rand_augment`.

Non-Monotonic Variant
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

The :func:`get_rand_augment_non_monotonic_suite` returns an alternative suite where some operations behave differently:

- ``brightness``, ``contrast``, ``color``, ``sharpness`` use a range of (0.1, 1.9), centered around 1.0, meaning strength is lowest at the center and increases toward the edges.
- ``posterize`` strength decreases with increasing magnitude (from 8 to 4 bits).
- ``solarize`` threshold increases with magnitude (from 0 to 256), meaning less aggressive inversion at higher magnitudes.

This variant mimics implementations found in other frameworks such as TensorFlow/TPU codebases.

Usage Example
-------------

Apply RandAugment with 2 operations of magnitude 10 from 31 bins:

.. code-block:: python

    from nvidia.dali import fn
    from nvidia.dali.auto_aug import rand_augment

    # Input data: batch of images in HWC layout, uint8 dtype
    images = fn.decoders.image(...)
    augmented_images = rand_augment(images, n=2, m=10, num_magnitude_bins=31)

Exclude certain operations:

.. code-block:: python

    # Exclude rotate and solarize from the augmentation suite
    augmented_images = rand_augment(
        images,
        n=2,
        m=10,
        excluded=["rotate", "solarize"]
    )

Use per-sample dynamic shapes (e.g., for variable-sized images):

.. code-block:: python

    shapes = fn.shapes(images)  # Extract dynamic shape
    augmented_images = rand_augment(
        images,
        n=2,
        m=10,
        shape=shapes,
        max_translate_rel=0.3
    )

Custom Augmentation List
------------------------

To use a custom list of augmentations, use :func:`apply_rand_augment` directly:

.. code-block:: python

    from nvidia.dali.auto_aug import augmentations as a

    custom_augmentations = [
        a.brightness.augmentation((0, 0.6), True, a.shift_enhance_range),
        a.rotate.augmentation((0, 45), True),
        a.auto_contrast,
    ]

    augmented_images = apply_rand_augment(
        augmentations=custom_augmentations,
        data=images,
        n=2,
        m=15,
        num_magnitude_bins=31
    )

Notes
-----

- All input samples must be of type ``uint8`` and have layout ``HWC`` (images) or ``FHWC`` (videos).
- The ``fill_value`` parameter controls padding for affine transformations; if ``None``, border values are repeated.
- When using ``shape``, translation magnitudes are interpreted as fractions of image dimensions.
- The ``seed`` parameter ensures reproducibility of operation selection and sign randomization.
- The ``excluded`` parameter only works with the default augmentation suites. For full control, use :func:`apply_rand_augment` with a manually defined list.

RandAugment

RandAugment, as described in https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.13719, is an
automatic augmentation scheme that simplified the AutoAugment. For
RandAugment the policy is just a list of
augmentations <Augmentation operations> with a search space limited to
two parameters n and m.

-   n describes how many randomly selected augmentations should we apply
    to an input sample.
-   m is a fixed magnitude used for all of the augmentations.

For example, to use 3 random operations for each sample, each with fixed
magnitude 17, you can call
~nvidia.dali.auto_aug.rand_augment.rand_augment, as follows:

    from nvidia.dali import pipeline_def
    from nvidia.dali.auto_aug import rand_augment

    @pipeline_def(enable_conditionals=True)
    def training_pipe(data_dir, image_size):

        jpegs, labels = fn.readers.file(file_root=data_dir, ...)
        shapes = fn.peek_image_shape(jpegs)
        images = fn.decoders.image(jpegs, device="mixed", output_type=types.RGB)

        augmented_images = rand_augment.rand_augment(images, shape=shapes, n=3, m=17)

        resized_images = fn.resize(augmented_images, size=[image_size, image_size])

        return resized_images, labels

The ~nvidia.dali.auto_aug.rand_augment.rand_augment uses set of
augmentations described in the paper. To apply custom augmentations
refer to this section <Invoking custom RandAugment policies>.

Warning

You need to define the pipeline with the
@pipeline_def <nvidia.dali.pipeline_def> decorator and set
enable_conditionals to True to use automatic augmentations.

Invoking custom RandAugment policies

Thanks to the simpler nature of RandAugment, its policies are defined as
lists of augmentations <Augmentation operations>, that can be passed as
a first argument to the
~nvidia.dali.auto_aug.rand_augment.apply_rand_augment when invoked
inside a pipeline definition.

NumPy provides enhanced distutils functionality to make it easier to
build and install sub-packages, auto-generate code, and extension
modules that use Fortran-compiled libraries. To use features of NumPy
distutils, use the setup <core.setup> command from numpy.distutils.core.
A useful Configuration
<misc_util.Configuration> class is also provided in
numpy.distutils.misc_util that can make it easier to construct keyword
arguments to pass to the setup function (by passing the dictionary
obtained from the todict() method of the class). More information is
available in the distutils-user-guide.

The choice and location of linked libraries such as BLAS and LAPACK as
well as include paths and other such build options can be specified in a
site.cfg file located in the NumPy root repository or a .numpy-site.cfg
file in your home directory. See the site.cfg.example example file
included in the NumPy repository or sdist for documentation.

Configuration class

Construct a configuration instance for the given package name. If
parent_name is not None, then construct the package as a sub-package of
the parent_name package. If top_path and package_path are None then they
are assumed equal to the path of the file this instance was created in.
The setup.py files in the numpy distribution are good examples of how to
use the Configuration instance.

Building Installable C libraries

Conventional C libraries (installed through add_library) are not
installed, and are just used during the build (they are statically
linked). An installable C library is a pure C library, which does not
depend on the python C runtime, and is installed such that it may be
used by third-party packages. To build and install the C library, you
just use the method add_installed_library instead of add_library, which
takes the same arguments except for an additional install_dir argument:

    .. hidden in a comment so as to be included in refguide but not rendered documentation
      >>> import numpy.distutils.misc_util
      >>> config = np.distutils.misc_util.Configuration(None, '', '.')
      >>> with open('foo.c', 'w') as f: pass

    >>> config.add_installed_library('foo', sources=['foo.c'], install_dir='lib')

npy-pkg-config files

To make the necessary build options available to third parties, you
could use the npy-pkg-config mechanism implemented in numpy.distutils.
This mechanism is based on a .ini file which contains all the options. A
.ini file is very similar to .pc files as used by the pkg-config unix
utility:

    [meta]
    Name: foo
    Version: 1.0
    Description: foo library

    [variables]
    prefix = /home/user/local
    libdir = ${prefix}/lib
    includedir = ${prefix}/include

    [default]
    cflags = -I${includedir}
    libs = -L${libdir} -lfoo

Generally, the file needs to be generated during the build, since it
needs some information known at build time only (e.g. prefix). This is
mostly automatic if one uses the Configuration method
add_npy_pkg_config. Assuming we have a template file foo.ini.in as
follows:

    [meta]
    Name: foo
    Version: @version@
    Description: foo library

    [variables]
    prefix = @prefix@
    libdir = ${prefix}/lib
    includedir = ${prefix}/include

    [default]
    cflags = -I${includedir}
    libs = -L${libdir} -lfoo

and the following code in setup.py:

    >>> config.add_installed_library('foo', sources=['foo.c'], install_dir='lib')
    >>> subst = {'version': '1.0'}
    >>> config.add_npy_pkg_config('foo.ini.in', 'lib', subst_dict=subst)

This will install the file foo.ini into the directory package_dir/lib,
and the foo.ini file will be generated from foo.ini.in, where each
@version@ will be replaced by subst_dict['version']. The dictionary has
an additional prefix substitution rule automatically added, which
contains the install prefix (since this is not easy to get from
setup.py). npy-pkg-config files can also be installed at the same
location as used for numpy, using the path returned from get_npy_pkg_dir
function.

Reusing a C library from another package

Info are easily retrieved from the get_info function in
`numpy.distutils.misc_util`:

    >>> info = np.distutils.misc_util.get_info('npymath')
    >>> config.add_extension('foo', sources=['foo.c'], extra_info=info)
    <numpy.distutils.extension.Extension('foo') at 0x...>

An additional list of paths to look for .ini files can be given to
get_info.

Conversion of .src files

NumPy distutils supports automatic conversion of source files named
<somefile>.src. This facility can be used to maintain very similar code
blocks requiring only simple changes between blocks. During the build
phase of setup, if a template file named <somefile>.src is encountered,
a new file named <somefile> is constructed from the template and placed
in the build directory to be used instead. Two forms of template
conversion are supported. The first form occurs for files named
<file>.ext.src where ext is a recognized Fortran extension (f, f90, f95,
f77, for, ftn, pyf). The second form is used for all other cases. See
templating.
